en: The *Suprabhāta-stotra* composed by King Śrī Harṣadeva:
"Though praised even by the hosts of gods, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas..."
On earth and in heaven, by the lords of ascetics with most diverse words of praise, I too, having exerted my power, bow to the noble Sambuddha;
when Garuḍa has taken flight into the sky, do not even the bees fly after him? (1)
He has destroyed the faction of evil, his defects are entirely exhausted, his complexion is like molten gold, and his eyes are as long as full-blown lotuses;
he possesses a most beautiful halo and the splendor of a radiant circle of light.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 2 ||
To the conqueror of the power of passion, the destroyer of evil paths, the benefactor of the three worlds, the remover of the thicket of the creeper of womanhood,
the bestower of the fruit of equal happiness, and the shatterer of the mountain of ignorance—
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 3 ||
He who is the first-born among asuras, suras, and humans, the preeminent deity,
the sole word for the creation of the worlds within the entire realm of existence—
the self-existent Lotus-born Creator of mankind— now sleeps.
O You who possess the ten powers, may your dawn always be a beautiful dawn. || 4 ||
Standing on the slope of the eastern mountain, copper-red like a slice of coral,
the sun— the single eye of all creatures and the destroyer of masses of darkness— is likewise entirely asleep, as if intoxicated with wine.
O possessor of the ten powers, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 5 ||
The moon, white as the tusk of an elephant, the cool-rayed one who is the crest-jewel of all and the tilaka-mark of the night—
even he has slept entirely, his intoxicating glow unabated.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak.
Even that Brahmā, who possesses four powerful arms, eight faces,
is conversant with the rules for recitation and observances, is the expounder of the Sāmaveda,
and whose source is the stainless lotus— has fallen fast asleep.
O Ten-Powered One, may your dawn always be a beautiful awakening. || 7 ||
Seated upon the peak of the Snowy Mountain, wearing a serpent as his sacred thread, skilled in the incineration of the three cities, and clad in an upper garment of tiger skin—
that wielder of the trident also lies asleep together with the daughter of the foremost of mountains.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 8 ||
Even the Lord of the Gods, though holding a blazing thunderbolt in his hand and invincible to the Dānavas, had his mind deluded by the charms of Śacī;
he slept day and night, submerged in the mire of passion.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 9 ||
Blue as the petal of a water-lily, with eyes as broad as white lotuses, the slayer of the hosts of the enemies of the gods, the creator of the universe and the one whose form is the universe—
even Hari, though long asleep, remains unreleased from dwelling in a womb.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 10 ||
Lord Paśupati, with his mass of matted hair tawny like a Kapila cow and his eyes crimson and copper-red, is uniquely skilled at severing unions even at the most inopportune time;
yet even he, his body shattered by the arrows of Smara, has fallen asleep like a sacrificial fire.
O Possessor of the Ten Powers, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 11 ||
Resembling a cloud, the moon, or a white water-lily, with eyes reddened from drinking wine,
his limbs and arms firm and hard, holding a plow and a spear in hand—
there Baladeva lies here, his neck entwined around Revatī.
O You who possess the ten powers, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 12 ||
The elephant-faced one, the sole destroyer of obstacles from all sides,
with ichor flowing from his temples and swarms of bees clustering there,
even Gaṇapati himself slept, intoxicated by the drinking of wine.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 13 ||

That son of the Three-eyed One, Kumāra, who is blue as the *atasī* flower, whose spear at the tip of his hand has the form of a fresh lotus, who is six-faced, the slayer of Krauñca, and who is eternally asleep; [may he protect you].
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 14 ||
Deprived of food and clothing, being emaciated and deformed, they are utterly beset by all manner of afflictions; like ghosts with burnt bodies,
devoid of both [human and divine] destinies, they lie asleep, naked.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 15 ||
O sages, even the great ones here— Vatsa, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and others;
Kratu, Pulaha, Vasiṣṭha, Vyāsa, Vālmīki, and Garga—
even they fell asleep, deluded by the charms of another's young wife.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 16 ||
Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, the lords of the Yakṣas, Daityas, and Uragas,
as well as the other guardians of the world in heaven, on earth, or in the sky—
even they have fallen asleep when gazed upon by the intoxicating side-long glances of young women.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 17 ||
Immersed in the ocean of existence, their bodies shrouded by the net of delusion—
Manu, Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others, whose minds are bewildered and who lack both equanimity and true happiness— those fools are likewise asleep.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. || 18 ||
Sleeping upon the vast bed of craving, with sense-objects as its pillow, in the darkness of the night of ignorance,
while the fruits of good and evil deeds are being scattered [upon her], she slumbers on.
Salutations to him who remains ever awake. || 19 ||
At sacred fords, hundreds of herds of cows drink the water and attain satisfaction, yet it does not undergo depletion;
even so, O Sage, is it with one who is praised by hundreds of poets.
The treasure-house of virtues of this ocean of qualities is never exhausted. || 20 ||
A beautiful dawn belongs only to you, whose eye is opened by wisdom;
for those blinded by the darkness of ignorance, the sun has forever set. (21)
Again there is dawn, again the sun has risen, again the moon, and again the night;
likewise, O Sage, death, old age, and birth—the coming and going—yet the deluded person does not perceive it. (22)
May there be a beautiful dawn and auspicious stars, greeted with glory;
day after day, I pay homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. (23)

Having praised the Teacher of the World, the supreme great sage— the source of the merit of the True Dharma, free from dualities, who has destroyed the darkness of passion and hatred, whose senses are tranquil, and who is desireless— may the entire world, by the very merit that I have thus acquired, [attain liberation].
Gladdened by the praise at dawn, may they find supreme faith in the One of Ten Powers. || 24 ||
The *Suprabhātastotra* of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, composed by King Śrī Harṣadeva, is completed.
